> Gcore is the second public neocloud repricing in a week. NBIS announced ~30% across the H100, H200, B200, B300 lineup last week; Gcore today.

>
> The spot/on-demand discount narrowed sharply at Gcore. H100: 45% to 28%. H200: 34% to 17%.
> That discount is the price of accepting preemption risk. Spot capacity is reclaimable at the provider's discretion. When the discount shrinks, the provider is repricing the implicit probability of reclaim, which only rises when on-demand demand is tight enough to make spot's underlying capacity worth pulling back.
>
> When the spot discount halves in a single repricing, spot is not functioning as a market. It is reflecting reclaim risk, not price discovery. The short-end clearing tier the procurement paradigm needs still doesn't exist. What looks like one is a kick-out option in disguise.

results.title: Vast.ai vs RunPod 2026: GPU Rental Marketplace Showdown | ServerRental
highlights:
## TL;DR

- Vast.ai wins on price – verified hosts offer RTX 3090 from $0.21/hr, H100 SXM from $2.00/hr, and median A100 80GB (PCIE) at $0.90/hr. RunPod’s community cloud is often 20–40% more expensive on comparable GPUs.
- RunPod wins on reliability – its Secure Cloud provides guaranteed uptime and persistent storage, while Vast.ai’s interruptible instances can be reclaimed without notice.
- Best for budget-conscious researchers & batch jobs – Vast.ai; best for production inference & long-running workloads – RunPod Secure Cloud.

...

## Pricing Comparison (H100, A100, RTX 4090)

Below is a direct price comparison for the most popular GPUs. Vast.ai prices are live as of Q2 2026 from verified hosts (minimum, median, maximum per GPU per hour). RunPod prices are approximate on-demand rates as published in 2026.

| GPU Model | Vast.ai Min | Vast.ai Median | Vast.ai Max | RunPod Community Cloud | RunPod Secure Cloud |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| NVIDIA A100 80GB (PCIE) | $0.66 | $0.90 | $1.53 | $1.19 – $1.99 | $1.49 – $2.49 |
| NVIDIA A100 SXM4 | $0.76 | $2.00 | $2.16 | $1.39 – $2.29 | $1.89 – $2.99 |
| NVIDIA H100 PCIe | $2.72 | $2.72 | $2.72 | $1.99 – $2.99 | $2.39 – $3.49 |
| NVIDIA H100 SXM | $2.00 | $2.80 | $4.44 | $2.19 – $3.19 | $2.59 – $3.89 |
| NVIDIA RTX 4090 | $0.67 | $0.93 | $10.37 | $0.34 – $0.69 | $0.69 – $1.29 |
| RTX 5090 | $1.01 | $1.67 | $53.34 | $1.09 – $1.99 | $1.49 – $2.49 |
| RTX A6000 (or RTX 6000 Ada) | $1.00 | $1.00 | $1.00 | $0.49 – $0.79 | $0.79 – $1.19 |

Key observations: For the H100 PCIe, Vast.ai median is $2.72/hr – higher than RunPod Community Cloud’s $1.99 entry point, but Vast.ai has only one verified offer (the median equals that single price). RunPod’s Secure Cloud H100 PCIe starts at $2.39/hr, cheaper than Vast.ai’s $2.72. However, for A100 80GB, Vast.ai’s median PCIE price of $0.90/hr is significantly below RunPod’s lowest community rate of $1.19/hr. The RTX 4090 is where Vast.ai shines: median $0.93/hr vs RunPod Community’s $0.34–$0.69 range (RunPod is cheaper on the low end). Overall, Vast.ai tends to be cheaper for older or less popular GPUs; for cutting‑edge H100s, RunPod’s community cloud can be more competitive.

...

Vast.ai is a pure peer-to-peer marketplace. Individual hosts (data centers, miners, or hobbyists) list their GPUs and set prices. Users filter by region, GPU type, disk size, and uptime. The platform charges a small fee on top of the host price. This model drives competition downward – hosts lower prices to win jobs, especially for idle hardware. The downside is variability: prices can spike when demand surges, and hosts may go offline without warning.

RunPod uses a hybrid approach. Its Community Cloud mirrors Vast.ai’s marketplace: hosts (usually data center partners) rent out GPUs. RunPod sets floor prices and takes a cut. Its Secure Cloud is operated entirely by RunPod in colocation facilities with fixed hourly rates, guaranteed availability, and persistent storage. Secure Cloud is billed per second and supports preconfigured templates for popular frameworks (PyTorch, TensorFlow, ComfyUI). This model provides predictable pricing and strong SLAs (99.9% uptime), but prices are typically 30–80% higher than Vast.ai’s most competitive community offers.

...

Vast.ai offers two types of instances: on-demand (hosts commit to not reclaim) and interruptible (host can terminate at any time if they need the GPU back). The price difference can be 2–3×. In practice, many hosts reclaim interruptible instances without notice, especially for consumer GPUs like RTX 3090/4090. For training jobs that checkpoint frequently, interruptible is viable; for long training runs or production inference, you must pay for on-demand or risk losing progress.

results.title: What Is a NeoCloud? GPU Cloud vs Hyperscalers (2026)
highlights:
- 1 A neocloud is a cloud provider built exclusively around GPU compute for AI workloads. CoreWeave, Lambda Labs, RunPod, and Vast.ai are the largest. They offer no general-purpose cloud services, no databases, no serverless, no managed application tiers: just GPUs, InfiniBand networking, and NVMe storage.
- 2 H100 80GB on-demand pricing on neoclouds runs $2.50-$4.00 per GPU-hour in Q2 2026 versus $6.88/hr on AWS and $12.29/hr on Azure for the same GPU. Across a 1,000 GPU-hour training job, that difference is $3,890 to $9,900 in savings depending on the provider (Spheron Network / Thunder Compute, May-June 2026).
- 3 Neoclouds suit GPU-intensive AI training and large-batch inference. They do not replace hyperscalers for general IT infrastructure, compliance-heavy enterprise workloads, or applications that need hundreds of managed cloud services alongside compute.

results.title: The AI infrastructure boom should not be funded through customer price hikes
highlights:
Reports paint a clear picture. Hyperscalers collectively spent hundreds of billions on capital expenditures in 2025 alone, with projections for 2026 pushing toward $600 billion globally - a nearly 40% jump in many cases, largely fuelled by AI build-outs. Those investments are starting to ripple through the entire technology stack. Major cloud providers and analysts have already warned that the cost of running infrastructure is set to rise, with some providers already adjusting pricing for GPU instances, data transfer, and specialised AI services. Reports point to increases of up to 15% on certain ML workloads, with further changes expected in core services. While some providers are still absorbing the pressure, many have indicated that pass-through increases will be unavoidable as margins tighten. “iOCO Cloud is taking a different approach. We are not passing these increased infrastructure costs on to our customers. “This isn’t a gesture, it’s a principle. Customers shouldn’t have to pay more every time the cloud infrastructure market shifts. Our job is to manage that complexity for them, not pass the problem on,” says Richard Vester, Executive: Cloud at iOCO.

...

Vester says the difference lies in how the environment is built and managed. By operating large-scale, multi-tenant cloud platforms, investing in its own infrastructure, and working across multiple cloud providers, iOCO is able to manage cost pressure in ways that many providers simply can’t. “When you run at scale, and you own part of the infrastructure as well as using hyperscalers, you have far more flexibility. You can optimise architecture, shift workloads, invest ahead of demand, and spread cost across environments. That’s how you protect customers from volatility instead of billing them for it,” he says. “Support costs, licensing, infrastructure – everything is getting more expensive. Simply passing those increases on to customers isn’t a strategy. The strategy is helping them run what they already have more efficiently, making better decisions about where workloads sit, eliminating wasted capacity, and only investing in new infrastructure when there’s a clear operational reason to do it.” Vester says the current pricing pressure is revealing how easily organisations can be pushed into higher spend without revisiting the fundamentals of their architecture. “When costs go up, the default advice is often to buy more, upgrade, or move to the next platform. That doesn’t always mean it’s the right move. The AI-driven cost surge is actually an opportunity to step back, assess what you’re running today, and make smarter decisions about placement, utilisation, and design before committing to more spend.” “Most organisations already have the platforms they need. What they often lack is the architecture, governance, and optimisation to unlock their full value. When infrastructure costs rise, the answer isn’t panic buying or simply spending more. It’s designing smarter, placing workloads properly, and working with a partner who can see the whole environment. The bottom line is that customers shouldn’t be funding the industry’s growth,” Vester concludes. If rising cloud costs are creating uncertainty, it may be time to reassess how your environment is designed, governed, and optimised.
